tasks.spec:
You are a READ-ONLY reviewer mapping how time flows through a video podcast production pipeline. The three source files you are reviewing have been staged INSIDE your own working directory at ./source/server/pipeline/ -- they are orchestrator.py (6,708 lines), av_sync.py (638 lines) and video_assembly.py (1,241 lines). Read them from there. You must NOT modify, create, or delete any file except ./report.md in your working directory, and you must not modify anything under ./source. Do not run git. Do not commit. Do not call any MCP tool or App. Do not capture anything to any external system.

BACKGROUND. This is the media pipeline for a two-person video podcast. Every episode begins as four separate WebM files recorded by a Daily.co room: host camera audio, host camera video, guest camera audio, guest camera video. Each file starts whenever that device joined the call, so the four files do not share a zero. In the reference episode the host tracks start at 0.225s and 0.229s while the guest tracks start at 224.875s and 224.896s, because the guest joined 224.7 seconds late. The tracks also contain dropouts, meaning stretches where packets stopped arriving: host audio has one 76.860s hole at 151.859s, and host video has thirteen holes totalling 219.960s including a 203.887s frozen stretch starting at 25.713s.

A module was just added that handles this correctly. In av_sync.py, derive_timeline() computes ONE session grid with T=0 at the earliest packet across all four tracks, measures every dropout as a packet hole, and build_stems() renders four stems that are all exactly the same length on that grid, with dropouts HELD (silence for audio, frozen frame for video) and never removed. It writes a timeline.json describing the grid, the per-track offsets onto the grid, and every hole.

THE PROBLEM YOU ARE MAPPING: nothing consumes any of that. The rest of the pipeline still re-derives its own timing from the raw WebM files. Five consecutive renders of the reference episode shipped with broken audio as a result.

YOU ARE THE INDEPENDENT SECOND READER. Another model is reviewing this same surface in parallel. Do not try to agree with anyone. The value of your report is the things a different reader would miss, so be exhaustive about finding EVERY site rather than explaining the first one you find beautifully.

ANSWER THESE FIVE QUESTIONS. Anchor every claim to a file and line you actually read.
1. Every site where sync offsets are derived, and from exactly which inputs. Name the function and the line. There is more than one such site; find all of them, and say how many you found.
2. Every site where the composite video is built, and exactly which media files it reads. Again, there is more than one; find all of them.
3. What an offset MEANS dimensionally at each site: relative to which zero, and in which direction (does a positive value delay or advance that track). If two sites disagree about the sense of the number, say so loudly, because that is the class of bug we are hunting.
4. What specifically would have to change for the composite to read the four stems plus timeline.json instead of the raw files, and what currently depends on the existing offsets that would break when it does.
5. Any code path where a fallback, a default, an exception handler, or a cached value could silently re-enter raw-track derivation after the rewire. These are the highest value findings in this lane.

DO NOT propose a patch and do not write code. Map what exists.

OUTPUT CONTRACT: write ./report.md in your working directory. Open with a two sentence summary of the surface. Then one section per question above, numbered 1 to 5. Every finding must carry a citation in the form server/pipeline/FILE.py:LINE -- write the path WITHOUT the leading ./source/ prefix, and use real line numbers you read from the staged files. Invented line numbers are checked against the real files and will fail. Cite at least eight distinct locations across the report. Where you are uncertain, say so and name what you would have to run to settle it.
